learningObjectives.title: The Wall Street Crash and the Depression

questions.q: Which mass-production method did Henry Ford use to manufacture cars quickly and cheaply?
questions.explain: Ford's moving assembly line allowed cars to be built faster and more cheaply, cutting prices and boosting demand.

questions.q: Which car became the best-selling symbol of mass production in 1920s America?
questions.explain: The mass-produced Model T became affordable for ordinary Americans and drove the growth of related industries.

questions.q: President Coolidge's saying 'the business of America is business' best reflects which government approach?
options: Laissez-faire, leaving business largely free from government interference
Heavy regulation of factories and wages
Free trade with no import tariffs
questions.explain: Republican governments followed laissez-faire, keeping taxes and regulation low to encourage business growth.

questions.q: Why did the growth of buying 'on credit' (hire purchase) help fuel the boom?
options: It let people buy goods immediately and pay in instalments, raising demand
It forced shops to lower all their prices by law
It banned the sale of foreign goods
It gave farmers higher prices for their crops
questions.explain: Hire purchase allowed consumers to buy cars and household goods they could not otherwise afford, increasing sales.

questions.q: Why did farmers largely fail to share in the prosperity of the 1920s?
options: Overproduction pushed crop prices down, leaving many in debt
Tariffs made it too cheap to import food
A ban on machinery stopped them farming
questions.explain: Agricultural overproduction caused prices to collapse, so many farmers earned less and struggled with debt.

questions.q: A 1925 family buys a new radio, paying a small deposit and the rest in monthly instalments. This best illustrates which feature of the boom?
questions.explain: Paying by instalments is hire purchase (credit), a key driver of rising consumer demand in the 1920s.

questions.q: Which constitutional amendment introduced prohibition, banning the sale of alcohol from 1920?
questions.explain: The 18th Amendment, enforced by the Volstead Act, banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol from 1920.

questions.q: What name was given to the illegal bars where people drank alcohol during prohibition?
questions.explain: Speakeasies were hidden, illegal bars where alcohol was sold despite prohibition.

questions.q: Which Chicago gangster became notorious for controlling bootlegging during prohibition?
questions.explain: Al Capone ran a criminal empire in Chicago based on illegal alcohol and other rackets during prohibition.

questions.q: Which amendment gave American women the right to vote in 1920?
questions.explain: The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, granted women the right to vote across the USA.

questions.q: Why are 'flappers' often used as evidence of changing attitudes towards women in the 1920s?
options: They challenged traditional norms by wearing shorter skirts, smoking and socialising freely
They campaigned to bring back prohibition
They led the Ku Klux Klan
They ran the major car factories
questions.explain: Flappers symbolised new social freedoms for some (mainly younger, urban) women that broke with earlier conventions.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why prohibition proved difficult to enforce?
options: Widespread bootlegging, corruption and demand for alcohol undermined the law
The government spent huge sums training enough agents
Almost no Americans wanted to drink alcohol
Alcohol was too expensive to smuggle
questions.explain: Continued demand, organised crime and bribery of officials made prohibition largely unenforceable.

questions.q: What does the revival of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s reveal about American society?
options: Deep racial and religious intolerance persisted, especially against Black Americans
Racism had almost disappeared by the 1920s
The government had ended all segregation
questions.explain: The KKK's growth showed the continuing strength of racism and prejudice in 1920s America.

questions.q: A man in 1925 secretly brews whiskey and sells it to a speakeasy for profit. What term describes his activity?
questions.explain: Producing and selling alcohol illegally during prohibition was known as bootlegging.

questions.q: In which month and year did the Wall Street Crash take place?
questions.explain: Share prices collapsed on the New York stock exchange in October 1929, marking the Wall Street Crash.

questions.q: How did 'buying on the margin' help cause the Wall Street Crash?
options: Investors borrowed money to buy shares, so falling prices left them unable to repay
It banned people from selling any shares
It fixed share prices at a high level by law
It gave every worker free shares
questions.explain: Speculators bought shares largely with borrowed money, so when prices fell they faced huge debts and had to sell.

questions.q: What name was given to the shanty towns built by homeless people during the Depression?
questions.explain: The makeshift settlements were mockingly named 'Hoovervilles' after President Hoover, blamed for the Depression.

questions.q: Why did unemployment rise sharply after the Wall Street Crash?
options: Falling demand and bank failures forced businesses to close or cut workers
The government banned people from working
questions.explain: As spending collapsed and banks failed, firms went bankrupt or laid off workers, driving unemployment up.

questions.q: In late 1929 an investor who bought shares with borrowed money finds their value has collapsed. What is the most likely consequence for him?
options: He is left owing money he cannot repay
He is guaranteed a government refund
His shares automatically double in value
He is given a job by the bank
questions.explain: Buying on the margin meant that when share prices fell the investor still owed the money he had borrowed.

questions.q: An unemployed family in 1931 loses their home and moves into a shack on the edge of the city. This scene best illustrates which effect of the Depression?
options: The growth of Hoovervilles and homelessness
The success of the economic boom
The rise of the assembly line
questions.explain: Mass unemployment and evictions during the Depression forced families into shanty towns called Hoovervilles.
